item.title: Why Imperfectly Correlated Assets Shrink Portfolio Risk
item.summary: When two assets do not move in perfect lockstep, their ups and downs partly cancel, so the portfolio is less volatile than a simple average of the assets' own volatilities would suggest. This is the core logic behind diversification and a frequent source of exam questions.

sections.heading: The intuition: cancelling swings
sections.body_markdown: Picture a shop that sells umbrellas and another that sells sunscreen. Rain hurts one and helps the other, so a person who owns both shops sees steadier total income than someone who owns only one. **Correlation** is the number that measures how closely two assets' returns move together. It runs from $-1$ (exactly opposite moves) through $0$ (no linear relationship) to $+1$ (perfect lockstep). Whenever the correlation is below $+1$, some of one asset's bad outcomes coincide with the other asset's average or good outcomes, and the combined return bounces around less.

sections.heading: What changes and what doesn't
sections.body_markdown:
Two separate facts:

- **Expected return** of a portfolio is just the weighted average of the assets' expected returns. Correlation has no effect on it.
- **Risk**, measured by standard deviation (the typical size of deviations from the average return), is *not* a weighted average, unless correlation is exactly $+1$. For any correlation below $+1$, portfolio standard deviation is **less than** the weighted average of the individual standard deviations.

So lower correlation gives you a free reduction in risk with the expected return untouched. The lower the correlation, the larger the reduction. At $\rho=+1$ there is none; at $\rho=-1$ the reduction is greatest and can reach zero risk with the right weights. Any $\rho<1$ helps, so negative correlation is not required.

sections.heading: Why the maths works: the covariance term
sections.body_markdown:
Portfolio variance is built from each asset's own variance plus a **covariance** term, which is how the two assets move together: $\text{Cov}_{1,2}=\rho_{1,2}\,\sigma_1\sigma_2$. For two assets:

$$\sigma_p^2=w_1^2\sigma_1^2+w_2^2\sigma_2^2+2w_1w_2\rho_{1,2}\sigma_1\sigma_2$$

Only the last term depends on correlation. A positive covariance adds to variance, a negative one subtracts from it. Setting $\rho=1$ makes the formula a perfect square, $(w_1\sigma_1+w_2\sigma_2)^2$, which is exactly the weighted average of the two standard deviations. Any smaller $\rho$ shrinks the last term and pulls the answer below that average.

sections.heading: Same-industry versus different-industry stocks, and the floor
sections.body_markdown:
Stocks in the same industry usually have high correlations because they face the same fuel costs, regulation and demand swings. Pairing two such stocks removes only the firm-specific (**idiosyncratic**) risk, not the shared industry risk, so the benefit is small. Pairing stocks from unrelated industries lowers risk much more.

Adding more and more assets keeps helping, but not without limit. In a large equal-weighted portfolio, the variance approaches the average covariance between the assets. The idiosyncratic risk fades out and what remains is **systematic (market) risk** that all the assets share. With stocks of standard deviation $\sigma$ and every pairwise correlation $\rho$, the portfolio standard deviation approaches $\sigma\sqrt{\rho}$, not zero.

worked_example.problem: A portfolio holds 50% in Asset X (standard deviation 20%) and 50% in Asset Y (standard deviation 30%). The correlation between X and Y is 0.20. These are given risk estimates, so no sample-versus-population choice arises. Find the portfolio standard deviation and compare it with the weighted average of the two standard deviations.
steps: Weighted average of the standard deviations: $0.5(20\%)+0.5(30\%)=25\%$. This is the answer you would get if $\rho=+1$.

BA II Plus: the calculator is in chain mode by default, so do not string the terms together. Enter 0.25 × 0.04 = STO 1; 0.25 × 0.09 = STO 2; 2 × 0.5 × 0.5 × 0.2 × 0.2 × 0.3 = STO 3. Then RCL 1 + RCL 2 + RCL 3 = (shows 0.0385) and press √x (shows 0.1962).
Interpretation: 19.62% is well below the 25% weighted average, and even below the 20% standard deviation of the less risky asset X.
worked_example.answer: The portfolio standard deviation is about 19.62%, below the 25% weighted average and below either asset's own standard deviation of 20% (X) or 30% (Y) in the case of X.

formulas.name: Two-asset portfolio standard deviation
formulas.where: $w_1,w_2$ are portfolio weights (summing to 1); $\sigma_1,\sigma_2$ are the assets' standard deviations; $\rho_{1,2}$ is their correlation; $\sigma_p$ is the portfolio standard deviation.

formulas.name: Covariance from correlation
formulas.where: $\text{Cov}_{1,2}$ is the covariance of the two assets' returns; $\rho_{1,2}$ their correlation; $\sigma_1,\sigma_2$ their standard deviations.

formulas.name: Perfect positive correlation (no benefit)
formulas.where: Portfolio standard deviation equals the weighted average of the individual standard deviations; weights $w_1,w_2$ are non-negative.

formulas.name: Perfect negative correlation
formulas.where: Risk is zero when $w_1=\sigma_2/(\sigma_1+\sigma_2)$; symbols as above.

exam_traps: Averaging the standard deviations. Portfolio standard deviation equals the weighted average only when $\rho=+1$; otherwise it is lower.
Believing diversification lowers expected return. Expected return is always the weighted average of the assets' expected returns, whatever the correlation.
Thinking you need negative correlation to reduce risk. Any correlation below $+1$ gives some reduction; negative values simply give more.
Dropping the factor 2 (or the correlation) in the covariance term when computing variance, or forgetting to take the square root at the end.
Assuming enough assets drive risk to zero. The portfolio keeps the systematic risk the assets share, so the floor reflects the average covariance.
builds_on: Mean, variance and standard deviation of returns

issues: flag overturned on second review: The numbers check out: 0.0100+0.0225+0.0060=0.0385 and its square root is about 19.62%. The formulas, the zero-risk weight at ρ=-1, the σ√ρ floor and the BA II Plus chain-mode note are all correct. The closing sentence is awkwardly worded, but its claim that 19.62% is below both 20% and 30% is true, so it teaches nothing wrong.

item.stem: A portfolio combines two risky assets whose returns have a correlation of exactly +1. Compared with the weighted average of the two assets' standard deviations, the portfolio standard deviation is:

options.text: Equal to the weighted average, so no risk reduction occurs
options.explanation: Correct. With $\rho=+1$ the variance formula collapses to $(w_1\sigma_1+w_2\sigma_2)^2$, so the standard deviation is exactly the weighted average.

options.text: Below the weighted average, because the assets differ in size
options.explanation: Mistake: believing that merely holding two different assets reduces risk. The reduction comes only from a correlation below +1.

options.text: Zero, because the assets move in perfect unison
options.explanation: Mistake: confusing +1 with −1. Zero risk is possible only with perfect negative correlation and suitable weights.

item.stem: A portfolio is split 50% / 50% between Asset A (standard deviation 10%) and Asset B (standard deviation 20%). The correlation of their returns is 0.25. These are given risk estimates. Compute the portfolio standard deviation, rounded to two decimals in percent.

options.explanation: Mistake: taking the weighted average of the standard deviations, which is only valid at $\rho=+1$.
Mistake: dropping the covariance term (treating correlation as zero), which gives $\sqrt{0.0125}$.

item.stem: An investor holds only airline stock A (standard deviation 30%). She will add an equal dollar amount of one of two candidates, each with a 30% standard deviation and the same expected return as A. Airline B has a 0.85 correlation with A; oil producer C has a 0.30 correlation with A. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Airline B reduces risk more, since its returns are driven by familiar shared factors
options.explanation: Mistake: equating familiarity or predictability with diversification. Shared drivers are exactly what keeps B's correlation with A high and leaves the risk in place.

options.text: Oil producer C reduces risk more, since its returns move less closely with A's
options.explanation: Correct. With equal standard deviations and weights, the lower correlation means a smaller covariance term and a lower portfolio standard deviation.

options.text: Both reduce risk equally, since the two candidates share the same standard deviation
options.explanation: Mistake: ignoring correlation. Equal individual risk does not mean equal contribution to portfolio risk.

item.stem: A fund holds 70% in Asset P (standard deviation 15%) and 30% in Asset Q (standard deviation 25%). The correlation between P and Q is 0.60. These are given risk estimates. Compute the portfolio standard deviation, rounded to two decimals in percent.

options.explanation: Mistake: using the weighted average $0.7(15)+0.3(25)$, which ignores that $\rho=0.6$ is below 1.
Mistake: omitting the factor 2 on the covariance term, which understates variance ($0.021375$ instead of $0.0261$).

issues: flag overturned on second review: Variance is 0.011025+0.005625+0.00945=0.0261, and its square root is 16.155%, which rounds to 16.16%. Distractor B (18%) is the weighted average. Distractor C (14.62%) comes from dropping the factor 2, which gives variance 0.021375. The key A is correct.

item.stem: A portfolio is held at fixed weights of 40% in asset M and 60% in asset N. The correlation between M and N falls from 0.8 to 0.2, while each asset's expected return and standard deviation stay the same. What happens to the portfolio?

options.text: Expected return falls and standard deviation falls
options.explanation: Mistake: believing that risk reduction must be paid for with lower expected return. Expected return depends only on weights and the assets' expected returns.

options.text: Expected return rises and standard deviation falls
options.explanation: Mistake: believing lower correlation raises the expected return. Correlation does not enter the expected-return formula.

options.text: Expected return is unchanged and standard deviation falls
options.explanation: Correct. Expected return is a weighted average and ignores correlation; the covariance term shrinks, lowering variance and standard deviation.

item.stem: A portfolio holds 60% in Asset X (standard deviation 20%) and 40% in Asset Y (standard deviation 30%). The correlation between X and Y is −0.5. Treat these as given risk estimates, so no sample or population divisor is needed. Compute the portfolio standard deviation, rounded to two decimals in percent.

options.explanation: Mistake: using the weighted average $0.6(20)+0.4(30)$, which is only valid when $\rho=+1$. This ignores the diversification benefit of the lower correlation.
Mistake: dropping the covariance term (treating $\rho=0$). Variance = 0.0144 + 0.0144 = 0.0288, giving 16.97%. This misses that negative correlation reduces risk further.

issues: solver chose B (high): With correlation -1, SD = |0.6*20 - 0.4*30| = |12 - 12| = 0. The weights do not make the SD 10%; the 0.00% option is correct.

item.stem: An investor splits money 50% / 50% between two funds, each with a standard deviation of 20%. The correlation between the funds is 0.50. These are given risk estimates. Compute the portfolio standard deviation, rounded to two decimals in percent.

options.explanation: Mistake: assuming no risk reduction, i.e. treating the correlation as +1 even though it is 0.50.
Mistake: treating the funds as uncorrelated (dropping the covariance term), giving $\sqrt{0.02}$.

item.stem: An investor holds an equal-weighted portfolio of n stocks. Every stock has a standard deviation of 10%, and every pair of stocks has a correlation of 0.40. As n grows from 2 to a very large number, what happens to the portfolio standard deviation?

options.text: It falls toward about 6.3%, a floor set by the shared covariance
options.explanation: Correct. Idiosyncratic risk is averaged away, but variance approaches the average covariance $0.4\times0.01=0.004$, giving $\sqrt{0.004}\approx6.3\%$.

options.text: It falls toward zero, since enough stocks remove every source of risk
options.explanation: Mistake: thinking diversification can eliminate all risk. Positive correlation means shared (systematic) risk remains.

options.text: It stays near 10%, since each stock has the same standard deviation
options.explanation: Mistake: assuming portfolio risk equals the individual stock risk. With $\rho<1$ the portfolio is less volatile than its parts.

item.front: What is the effect on portfolio standard deviation when two assets have a correlation of +1?
item.back: No risk reduction: portfolio standard deviation equals the weighted average of the two assets' standard deviations.

item.front: Why is portfolio standard deviation below the weighted average of individual standard deviations when correlation is less than 1?
item.back: The covariance term is smaller than in the perfect-correlation case, so the assets' swings partly offset each other.

item.front: Does lowering the correlation between two assets change the portfolio's expected return?
item.back: No. Expected return is the weighted average of the assets' expected returns; only portfolio risk changes.

item.front: What kind of risk remains in a large portfolio of positively correlated assets, and what sets its size?
item.back: Systematic (market) risk, determined by the average covariance among the assets. It cannot be diversified away.
